english: May I ask you for directions?
usage: May I ask you for directions?
Polite opener to a stranger; 여쭤보다 is the humble verb for 'ask (someone above me)'
Let me ask you for directions.
반말 to a friend or someone younger; plain 물어보다 instead of humble 여쭤보다
May I trouble you with a question?
격식 — very formal, to an older stranger or in a serious setting
Excuse me, may I ask you for directions?
Softest, most natural street version; 저기요 gets attention first
examples: 저기요, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요.
Excuse me, may I ask you for directions?
Open with 저기요 to flag a stranger before the question
죄송한데 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 시청이 어느 쪽이에요?
Sorry, may I ask directions? Which way is City Hall?
죄송한데 softens the interruption before you ask
실례합니다, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 제가 여기 처음이라서요.
Excuse me, may I ask for directions? It's my first time here.
Adding 처음이라서요 ('I'm new here') makes the request feel reasonable
nuance: This is the courteous opener a stranger uses before asking directions on the street, said to an adult you don't know. 여쭤보다 is the humble form of 물어보다 — it lowers you and raises the listener, which is exactly right when you're asking a favor of a stranger, so it sounds polite without being stiff. Shift down to 물어볼게 in 반말 with friends, or up to 여쭤보겠습니다 in 격식 with an elder. The nearest alternative is just 저기요, 말씀 좀 묻겠습니다, but 여쭤보다 is warmer; the dividing line is humility — 묻다 is neutral, 여쭤보다 actively honors the listener. The classic English-speaker mistake is launching straight into 'Where is...?' with no opener, which lands as abrupt; Koreans almost always cushion the question first.

mistakes: Saying 물어볼게요 to a stranger thinking it's polite — it's only neutral; the humble 여쭤보다 is what makes asking a favor sound respectful.
Skipping the opener and going straight to 시청 어디예요? — without 저기요/죄송한데 it sounds like a demand, not a request.
Using 여쭤보다 about yourself answering ('I'll 여쭤보 you the way') — it only works when YOU are the one asking upward, never when you give the answer.

usage: 존댓말 to a stranger; point at a map or address while you say 여기
반말 to a friend; same words, drop the 요
How am I supposed to get here?
Slightly more careful; 가야 돼요 = 'what do I have to do to get there'
What do I do to get here?
Natural alternative; 가려면 ('in order to go') frames it as 'to get there, what do I...'
examples: 여기 어떻게 가요?
How do I get here?
The bare question while pointing at the place on your phone
이 주소 여기 어떻게 가요? 걸어가도 돼요?
How do I get to this address? Can I walk?
Showing the 주소 (address) makes 여기 concrete
여기 어떻게 가요? 지하철로 가는 게 나아요, 버스가 나아요?
How do I get here? Is it better by subway or by bus?
Following up with options invites a fuller answer
nuance: This is the all-purpose 'how do I get there' you say to a passerby or station staff while pointing at a place — on a map, a screenshot, or a written address. 여기 ('here') works because you're showing the destination, not because you're standing at it; this trips up English speakers who expect 거기 ('there'). Politeness rides entirely on the ending: 가요? is friendly-polite for strangers, 가? is 반말, and 가야 돼요? sounds a touch more deferential. The closest alternative is 여기 어떻게 찾아가요? (how do I find my way there), which adds the nuance of locating a hidden spot; plain 어떻게 가요? just asks the route. The big mistake is translating 'How can I go?' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요?, which asks about ability/permission and sounds odd — Koreans ask 어떻게 가요? for the method.

mistakes: Saying 거기 어떻게 가요? while pointing at a map — when the destination is right in front of you on the screen, Koreans say 여기; 거기 implies a place neither of you can see.
Using 어떻게 갈 수 있어요? for 'how can I get there' — 갈 수 있어요 asks if it's POSSIBLE; for the route use plain 어떻게 가요?.
Dropping the particle and asking 여기 가요? alone — that sounds like 'are you going here?'; you need 어떻게 to mean 'by what route'.

usage: 존댓말 to a stranger; 여기서 = 여기에서 ('from here'), the starting point
반말 to a friend; just drop the 요
Is it very far from here?
많이 ('a lot') stresses you're worried about distance
The positive flip; ask 가까워요? when you're hoping it's near
examples: 여기서 멀어요?
Is it far from here?
The bare check after someone names your destination
남대문시장 여기서 멀어요? 걸어갈 만해요?
Is Namdaemun Market far from here? Is it walkable?
걸어갈 만해요 asks if it's 'worth walking' / manageable on foot
여기서 멀어요? 멀면 택시 탈게요.
Is it far from here? If it's far I'll take a taxi.
Stating your plan (멀면 택시) helps them gauge how to answer
nuance: You say this to a stranger or staff member right after they tell you where something is, to judge whether to walk or ride. 여기서 is the contracted 여기에서 and marks the starting point ('from here') — getting that 에서 vs 에 right matters, because 여기에 멀어요 is wrong. The register is set by the ending: 멀어요? polite, 멀어? casual. The natural opposite, 가까워요?, isn't just 'not far' — choose it when your tone is hopeful, and 멀어요? when you're bracing for bad news; that emotional lean is the real dividing line. English speakers often build 'Is it far?' as 그것은 멀어요? with an explicit subject, but Korean drops it — the bare 여기서 멀어요? is what people actually say, and stuffing in 그것은 sounds like a textbook.

Adding a subject like 거기 그곳은 멀어요? — Korean leaves it out; the bare 여기서 멀어요? is natural and complete.
Confusing 멀어요 with 머리 or 몰라요 in speech — 멀다 (far) conjugates to 멀어요; don't say 멀라요.

english: Can I get there on foot?
usage: Can I get there on foot?
존댓말 to a stranger; 걸어서 = 'on foot', 갈 수 있어요 = 'is it possible to go'
반말 to a friend; drop the 요
Is it okay to walk there?
Shorter, very common; 걸어가다 ('walk over') + 도 돼요 ('is it allowed/fine')
갈 만하다 asks if the walk is reasonable, not just physically possible
examples: 걸어서 갈 수 있어요?
Can I get there on foot?
The bare question when you'd rather not take transit
경복궁까지 걸어서 갈 수 있어요?
Can I walk all the way to Gyeongbokgung?
까지 ('all the way to') marks the destination of the walk
여기서 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? 아니면 버스 타야 돼요?
Can I walk from here? Or do I have to take a bus?
Offering the alternative (버스 타야 돼요) makes the answer easy to give
nuance: Said to a passerby or staff when you're deciding whether to walk instead of ride. 걸어서 literally means 'by walking' (걷다 + 어서, the means/manner connector), and 갈 수 있어요? asks possibility — together a clean 'is walking there an option?'. The very common shorter form 걸어가도 돼요? swaps in 도 돼요 ('is it okay'), which leans toward permission/advisability rather than raw distance; the dividing line is that 갈 수 있어요? asks 'is it feasible' while 갈 만해요? asks 'is it worth it'. Politeness is in the ending alone. The English-speaker trap is saying 걸을 수 있어요?, which means 'am I physically able to walk' (as in, are my legs okay) — you need the directional 걸어서 가다 ('walk THERE'), not bare 걷다.

Using 걸어서 갈게요 (a statement of intent) when you mean to ask — to ask possibility, keep the question 갈 수 있어요?.
Forgetting 서 and saying 걸어 갈 수 있어요? — the natural manner form is 걸어서 (걷다+어서); 걸어 alone sounds clipped.

usage: 존댓말 to a stranger; 걸리다 here = 'take (time)', not 'hang'
반말 to a friend; drop the 요
How much time does it take?
Adding 시간 ('time') makes it unambiguous you mean duration
How long does it take from here?
여기서 anchors the question to your current spot
examples: 얼마나 걸려요?
How long does it take?
The bare follow-up after they name a route
지하철로 얼마나 걸려요?
How long does it take by subway?
로 ('by means of') specifies the mode you're asking about
걸어서 가면 얼마나 걸려요? 한 십 분이면 돼요?
How long if I walk? Is about ten minutes enough?
Guessing a number (십 분) invites them to confirm or correct
nuance: This is the standard 'how long does it take' for travel time, said to anyone who knows the route. The verb 걸리다 carries the meaning 'take (time)' here — the same verb means 'hang' or 'catch (a cold)' elsewhere, so context does the work; pairing it with a mode like 지하철로 or 걸어서 keeps it clear. Politeness is the ending: 걸려요? polite, 걸려? casual, with no separate 격식 form usually needed for a quick street question. The nearest alternative, 시간이 얼마나 들어요?, uses 들다 and leans toward effort/cost of time; 걸리다 is the default for clock duration and is what you want. The frequent English-speaker error is asking 얼마예요? — that means 'how much (money)', not 'how long'; for time it must be 얼마나 걸려요.

Dropping 나 and asking 얼마 걸려요? — for 'how long/how much' of time you need 얼마나, not bare 얼마.

english: Which exit number do I go out?
usage: 존댓말 to staff or a passerby; 몇 번 = 'what number', 출구 = 'exit'
반말 to a friend; drop the 요
Which exit do I have to take?
나가야 돼요 ('have to go out') sounds a bit more careful
Shortest form when you just want the number
examples: 몇 번 출구로 나가요?
Which exit do I go out?
The bare question to a station worker
롯데백화점 가려면 몇 번 출구로 나가요?
Which exit for Lotte Department Store?
가려면 ('to get to') ties the exit to your destination
여기 시청역 맞죠? 몇 번 출구로 나가야 시청이 나와요?
This is City Hall Station, right? Which exit comes out at City Hall?
나와요 ('comes out') asks where the exit lands you
nuance: Korean subway exits are numbered (1번 출구, 2번 출구...), so this is the precise question you ask station staff or a fellow rider to find the right street exit. The particle 로 marks direction ('out THROUGH which exit'), which is why 출구로 나가다 is the set phrase; swapping in 에서 changes the meaning. Register is just the ending — 나가요? polite, 나가? casual. A close alternative is 몇 번 출구예요? when you only need the number and not the verb; the dividing line is that 나가요? asks the action of exiting while 출구예요? asks the label. English speakers often say 어느 출구 ('which exit') by analogy with English, but for a numbered set Koreans say 몇 번 ('what number') — 어느 출구 sounds like you're choosing among a few unnamed doors.

Saying 몇 출구 without 번 — the counter 번 is required after a number for exits: 몇 번 출구, not 몇 출구.

english: Does this go to City Hall?
usage: Does this (bus/train) go to City Hall?
존댓말 to the driver or a rider; 이거 = 'this one', the vehicle you're on/about to board
Does this go to City Hall?
반말 to a friend boarding with you
Does this bus go to City Hall?
이 버스 spells out the vehicle when 이거 might be unclear
Does this head toward City Hall?
쪽으로 ('in the direction of') when you just need the general direction
examples: 이거 시청 가요?
Does this go to City Hall?
Said to the bus driver as you step on
기사님, 이거 시청 가요?
Driver, does this go to City Hall?
기사님 ('driver, sir') is the polite address for a bus/taxi driver
이거 시청 가요? 시청에서 내리려고요.
Does this go to City Hall? I'm trying to get off at City Hall.
내리려고요 ('I intend to get off') explains why you're asking
nuance: This is the quick boarding check you fire at a bus driver or fellow passenger — 이거 ('this one') points at the very bus or train in front of you, and naming the stop (시청) is enough; you can drop the 에 because casual transit speech compresses it. Address the driver as 기사님 to sound polite. Register is the ending: 가요? polite, 가? casual. The near alternative 이거 시청 쪽으로 가요? asks general direction rather than 'stops there', useful when you only need to head that way; the dividing line is destination vs. direction. English speakers tend to ask 이것은 시청에 갑니까? — grammatically fine but stiff and slow for a doorway; real riders say the clipped 이거 시청 가요?. Also avoid 이거 시청 와요? — 오다 ('come') is wrong from the rider's side; the bus 가다 ('goes') there.

usage: 존댓말 to staff or a rider; 갈아타다 = 'change (vehicles)', 어디서 = 'at what place'
Where do I have to transfer?
갈아타야 돼요 ('have to change') is slightly more careful
Which line do I transfer to?
When you need the line number, not just the station; 호선 = 'subway line'
examples: 어디서 갈아타요?
Where do I transfer?
The bare question once you know you can't go direct
강남 가려면 어디서 갈아타요?
Where do I transfer to get to Gangnam?
가려면 ties the transfer point to the destination
이거 타고 가다가 어디서 갈아타야 돼요?
Riding this, where do I need to transfer?
가다가 ('while going, then') marks the switch mid-journey
nuance: You ask this of station staff or a knowledgeable rider when your trip needs a transfer. 갈아타다 is one word meaning 'change vehicles' (갈다 'replace' + 타다 'ride'), and the place takes 어디서 (어디에서, 'at what location') because the transfer happens AT a station. Politeness is the ending only. The related 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? asks which line to switch TO (note 으로, direction), versus 어디서 갈아타요? which asks the where; pick by whether you need the station or the line. The English-speaker pitfall is building it from 'change' as two ideas — 버스를 바꿔서 타요 sounds like you swap one ticket for another; the single verb 갈아타다 is the natural 'transfer'. Also don't use 어디에 갈아타요? — the action happens at a place, so it's 어디서, not 어디에.

usage: 존댓말 statement; also a request to let you through. 내리다 = 'get off/down'
Get off here. / I'm getting off here.
반말 to a friend, or telling them where to alight
내릴게요 ('I'll get off') warns the people blocking you so they move
Is this where we get off?
Same words as a question — checking with a companion or rider
examples: 여기서 내려요.
This is my stop.
Said as you stand up and edge toward the door
잠시만요, 여기서 내려요. 좀 지나갈게요.
Excuse me, this is my stop. Let me through.
잠시만요 + 지나갈게요 is the polite combo to part a crowded bus
다음에서 내려요? 아니요, 여기서 내려요.
Do we get off at the next one? No, we get off here.
Contrasting 다음 (next) with 여기 (here) pins down the stop
nuance: 내려요 covers both 'I'm getting off here' (a statement) and, on a packed bus, a polite signal for people to step aside. 여기서 (여기에서) marks the place the getting-off happens — 내리다 takes 에서 for the spot, never 에. Register is the ending: 내려요 polite, 내려 casual, and 내릴게요 ('I'll get off') is the softest, since the 게 ending frames it as a heads-up to others. English speakers often say 여기서 나가요 thinking 'get out' — but 나가다 is 'exit a building'; leaving a vehicle is 내리다.

usage: 존댓말 to a rider; 다음 역 = 'next station', for subway/train
반말 to a friend; 어디예요 → 어디야
For a BUS, use 정류장 ('stop'); 역 is for trains/subway
무슨 역 ('what station') when you want the name specifically
examples: 다음 역이 어디예요?
What's the next station?
The bare question to the person beside you
저기요, 다음 역이 어디예요? 제가 깜빡 졸아서요.
Excuse me, what's the next station? I dozed off.
깜빡 졸아서요 ('I nodded off') explains why you lost track
다음 역이 어디예요? 시청역 아직 멀었어요?
What's the next station? Is City Hall still far?
아직 멀었어요 ('still far?') asks how many stops remain
nuance: This is how you ask a fellow passenger which station comes next when you've lost the thread. Crucially, 역 means a train/subway station, so use it underground; on a bus the word is 정류장, and mixing them up marks you instantly as a foreigner. The variant 다음이 무슨 역이에요? specifically requests the station's name; 어디예요? can get either a name or a 'two more stops' answer — that's the dividing line. usage: 존댓말 statement or advice; 빠르다 = 'fast', irregular → 빨라요
At this hour the subway is faster.
Pinning it to rush hour; 이 시간엔 = 'at this time'
examples: 지하철이 빨라요.
The subway's faster.
Bare advice when someone asks bus vs. subway
버스보다 지하철이 빨라요. 길이 막혀서요.
The subway's faster than the bus — traffic's bad.
보다 ('than') sets up the comparison; 막혀서 explains why
지금은 지하철이 빨라요. 버스는 차 많이 막혀요.
Right now the subway's faster; buses get stuck in traffic.
Contrasting present conditions helps them choose

To make the comparison explicit, add 보다 ('than') on the slower option: 버스보다 지하철이 빨라요. Register is the ending only. A near alternative is 지하철이 더 나아요 ('the subway's better'), which is broader — it can mean cheaper, comfier, or faster — whereas 빨라요 is specifically about speed; choose by what you mean. usage: 존댓말 to a passerby; 정류장 = '(bus) stop'
버스 정류장 어디예요? / 정류장이 어디 있어요?
Where's the bus stop? / Where is there a stop?
어디 있어요 ('where is there') stresses you're searching for one
Same frame for the subway; swap 정류장 → 역
examples: 버스 정류장 어디예요?
Where's the bus stop?
The bare question to anyone on the street
저기요, 가까운 버스 정류장 어디예요?
Excuse me, where's the nearest bus stop?
가까운 ('nearest') narrows it to the closest one
151번 타는 버스 정류장 어디예요?
Where's the stop for the 151 bus?
151번 타는 ('where you catch the 151') ties the stop to a route

The English-speaker mistake is 버스 스탑 (a loanword) or 버스 역 — neither is idiomatic; it's 버스 정류장, often shortened to just 정류장.

usage: 존댓말 to a stranger; 길을 잃다 = 'lose one's way', past tense 잃었어요
잃어버리다 adds 'and it's done/gone', stressing you're really stuck
I don't know where I am.
Natural alternative; literally 'I don't know where here is'
examples: 길을 잃었어요.
I'm lost.
The bare admission when you stop someone for help
저기요, 길을 잃었어요. 시청역이 어느 쪽이에요?
Excuse me, I'm lost. Which way is City Hall Station?
Following with a concrete question gets you unstuck
관광하다가 길을 잃어버렸어요. 여기가 어딘지 모르겠어요.
I got lost while sightseeing. I don't know where I am.
Pairing both phrases makes your situation crystal clear
nuance: This is what you tell a stranger when you've lost your way and need help. The set phrase is 길을 잃다 ('lose the road'), with 길 taking the object particle 을 — and the past tense 잃었어요 is correct even though in English you say the present 'I am lost', because Korean treats the losing as a completed event. Adding 버리다 (잃어버렸어요) emphasizes it's irreversibly done and you're flustered. Register is the ending. The everyday alternative 여기가 어딘지 모르겠어요 ('I don't know where I am') is softer and very common; the dividing line is that 길을 잃었어요 names the predicament while 어딘지 모르겠어요 describes your confusion — many Koreans actually prefer the latter. The big mistake is the present tense 길을 잃어요, which sounds like a habit ('I lose my way [regularly]'); use the past 잃었어요.

Dropping the particle: 길 잃었어요 is okay casually, but in careful speech keep 길을 잃었어요.

usage: 존댓말 to a stranger; 이 근처 = 'this vicinity / around here'
반말 to a friend; 근처예요 → 근처야
맞아요 ('is that right') seeks confirmation of your guess
examples: 이 근처예요?
Is it around here?
The bare check when you think you're close
편의점 이 근처에 있어요?
Is there a convenience store around here?
Naming the target (편의점) + 있어요 asks if one exists nearby
제가 찾는 호텔이 이 근처예요? 주소는 이건데요.
Is the hotel I'm looking for around here? This is the address.
Showing the 주소 lets them place it relative to 'here'
nuance: You say this to a stranger to confirm whether your destination is in the immediate area. 근처 means 'vicinity/nearby', and 이 근처 ('this vicinity') points to where you both stand. The neighbor word 주변 ('surroundings') is nearly synonymous — 이 주변이에요? works too — but 근처 feels a touch closer/more colloquial; the line is small. The English-speaker mistake is reaching for 가까이 ('nearby', adverb) as a noun and saying 이 가까이예요?, which is ungrammatical; 가까이 modifies verbs (가까이 있어요), while the noun for 'the area nearby' is 근처. Also don't say 여기 근처 and 이 근처 interchangeably without care — both occur, but 이 근처 is the cleaner 'this vicinity'.

usage: 존댓말 instruction (what you'll HEAR); 쭉 = 'straight on, all the way'
반말 to a friend you're directing
직진 ('go straight', Sino-Korean) is more formal/road-sign-like
쭉 가다가 + 도세요 chains 'keep going, then turn'
examples: 쭉 가세요.
Just go straight.
The bare answer you'll get when the place is straight ahead
여기서 쭉 가세요. 그럼 왼쪽에 있어요.
Go straight from here, then it's on your left.
그럼 왼쪽에 ('then on the left') completes the directions you receive
이 길로 쭉 가다가 사거리에서 건너세요.
Go straight along this road, then cross at the intersection.
사거리 ('four-way intersection') + 건너세요 ('cross') is a common next step
nuance: 쭉 가세요 is mostly something you HEAR — a local telling you to keep going straight — but you'll also say it when directing someone. 쭉 is a vivid native adverb meaning 'straight on / all the way without stopping', warmer and more casual than the Sino-Korean 직진 (literally 'straight-advance'), which sounds like a driving-test or road-sign term; that formality is the dividing line. The instruction comes in 세요 (polite command), 직진하세요 (more formal), or 가 (반말). To extend, chain with 가다가 ('go, and then'): 쭉 가다가 오른쪽으로 도세요. The English-speaker trap is translating 'go straight' as 똑바로 가세요 — 똑바로 does mean 'straight', but it also means 'properly/upright', so it can sound like 'walk properly!'; for 'continue straight ahead' the natural word is 쭉 (or 직진). Also pair turns with 으로 (오른쪽으로 도세요), not 에.

usage: Please call a taxi for me.
존댓말 to hotel/restaurant staff; 부르다 = 'call/summon', 불러 주세요 = 'please call (for me)'
Could you call me a taxi, please?
주시겠어요 is more formal/softer — a polite request to staff
잡다 ('catch/hail') for flagging one on the street vs. 부르다 'phone/app one'
examples: 택시 좀 불러 주세요.
Please call me a taxi.
Said at a hotel front desk
죄송한데 택시 좀 불러 주시겠어요? 공항 가야 해서요.
Sorry, could you call me a taxi? I need to get to the airport.
공항 가야 해서요 ('I have to get to the airport') gives the reason
비 와서 그러는데, 택시 좀 불러 주세요.
It's raining, so could you call a taxi for me?
비 와서 그러는데 ('since it's raining') softens the request with context
nuance: This is the request you make to hotel, restaurant, or shop staff to summon a taxi for you. 부르다 means 'call/summon' (by phone or app), and 불러 주세요 adds 주다 ('do for me') to make it a favor — that 주세요 is what keeps it polite. Bump it up to 불러 주시겠어요? with staff for extra courtesy, or down to 불러 줘 with a friend. The English-speaker mistake is omitting 주세요 and saying just 택시 불러요, which sounds like you're narrating, not requesting — Korean marks 'for me, please' with 주세요. Also note 부르다 is 르-irregular: 불러, not 부르어.
